content.title: Identifying Relationships: Sequence, Contrast, and Cause-Effect
content.overview: This lesson focuses on identifying how ideas and events are connected within a text. By scanning for specific signal words and punctuation, you can determine if a sentence establishes a temporal sequence, a comparison/contrast, or a cause-effect relationship.
learning_objectives: Identify temporal sequence by recognizing chronological order signals.
Distinguish between comparison and contrast relationships using comparative signal words.
Recognize cause-effect relationships by identifying reasons and their resulting outcomes.
Apply the Relationship Signal Scan strategy to categorize sentence-level connections.

sections.title: The Relationship Signal Scan
sections.content: When the ACT Reading section asks about the relationship between two ideas or events, use the Relationship Signal Scan. First, spot signal words or punctuation that link clauses. Second, ask how one element affects the other: Does one happen before the other? Is one different from the other? Does one explain the other? Finally, label the relationship as Temporal, Contrast, or Cause-Effect based on the strongest signal.

sections.title: Temporal Sequence
sections.content: Temporal relationships show the order of events in time. They establish what happened earlier versus what happened later. Common signal words include: then, before, after, next, subsequently, previously, and while. Punctuation like semicolons followed by 'then' can also indicate a sequence.

sections.title: Comparison and Contrast
sections.content: Comparison/Contrast relationships show how two things are similar or different. Comparison signals include: like, similarly, and also. Contrast signals include: however, whereas, but, conversely, and compared with. These relationships often highlight a shift in perspective or a change in conditions.

sections.title: Cause and Effect
sections.content: Cause-Effect relationships show a reason (cause) and a result (effect). One event or idea is responsible for the occurrence of another. Common signal words include: because, so, therefore, as a result, consequently, and since. The 'cause' is the explanation, while the 'effect' is the outcome.

worked_examples.question: Identify the primary relationship in this sentence: 'The city implemented a new recycling program in January; consequently, the amount of landfill waste decreased by 20% by June.'
worked_examples.solution: 1. Scan for signal words: The word 'consequently' is found linking the two clauses. 2. Analyze the connection: The implementation of the program (action) explains why the waste decreased (result). 3. Label the relationship: This is a Cause-Effect relationship because 'consequently' signals a result stemming from a specific cause.

worked_examples.question: Identify the primary relationship in this sentence: 'While the first expedition focused on mapping the coastline, the second venture sought to establish inland trade routes.'
worked_examples.solution: 1. Scan for signal words: The word 'While' at the start of the sentence sets up a distinction between two subjects. 2. Analyze the connection: The sentence highlights the difference in goals between the first and second expeditions. 3. Label the relationship: This is a Comparison/Contrast relationship (specifically contrast) because it weighs two different objectives against each other.

common_mistakes: Confusing 'than' for a simple contrast when it is part of a cause-effect result (e.g., 'so... taller than'). Always look for the primary connector like 'so' or 'because' first.
Assuming all time-based words indicate sequence; sometimes 'while' indicates a contrast between two simultaneous but different actions rather than a chronological order.
Misidentifying the direction of cause-effect; ensure you know which part is the reason and which is the result.
exam_tips: If you see 'however' or 'but,' immediately look for a shift in the author's argument or a contrast between two facts.
When a question asks 'Why did X happen?', you are being asked to locate a Cause-Effect relationship.
Temporal sequence is not just about dates; look for transition words like 'finally' or 'initially' that organize the flow of a process.
content.recap: To master relationship questions, scan for signal words: 'then/after' for Temporal, 'however/compared with' for Contrast, and 'because/so' for Cause-Effect. Always verify that your chosen relationship matches the logic of how the two clauses interact.

knowledge_claims.content: A temporal sequence relationship shows the chronological order of events, identifying what happened earlier versus later.
Signal words such as 'then,' 'before,' 'after,' and 'subsequently' are primary indicators of a temporal sequence.
A comparison/contrast relationship identifies similarities or differences between two or more ideas, people, or events.
Signal words such as 'however,' 'whereas,' 'but,' and 'compared with' indicate a contrast relationship.
A cause-effect relationship demonstrates a reason-and-result connection where one event leads to another.
Signal words such as 'because,' 'so,' 'therefore,' and 'as a result' are primary indicators of a cause-effect relationship.
The first step in the Relationship Signal Scan is to spot signal words or punctuation that link two events, ideas, or clauses.
To verify a cause-effect relationship, identify which clause provides the reason and which clause provides the result.
A common mistake is focusing on a secondary comparison word like 'than' while ignoring a primary cause-effect connector like 'so'.
The word 'while' can signal either a temporal relationship (simultaneous events) or a contrast relationship (differing ideas), depending on context.
After labeling a relationship, re-read the clause following the signal word to confirm it matches the logic of the assigned label (Temporal, Contrast, or Cause-Effect).
The word 'consequently' is a high-level signal word specifically used to denote a cause-effect relationship.

items.stem:
PASSAGE A
Rina coordinated a community garden that allowed residents to borrow specialized materials. At first, Rina assumed that adding more items would increase use. A short survey, however, showed that many visitors were uncertain about how to begin. The survey became a compass: it pointed the team toward clearer labels and a one-page guide. During the next month, completed loans rose from 18 to 27. Rina concluded that the collection had not needed to become larger; it had needed to become easier to navigate.

PASSAGE B
A second coordinator, Eli, agreed that instructions matter but argued that conversation is equally important. At Eli's site, volunteers greet new visitors and demonstrate one tool before explaining the catalog. Eli views the catalog as a reference, not a substitute for human guidance.

TABLE: Completed loans
Before revision: 18
After revision: 27

Which event occurred immediately before the increase in completed loans?

options.C: The team introduced labels and a guide.
options.D: The initial assumption was proved correct without testing.

items.explanation: The keyed response follows the text and targets 识别时间顺序、比较对照和因果关系.

videoLesson.title: Label Temporal, Contrast, and Cause-Effect
videoLesson.description: Recognize if a sentence shows sequence, contrast, or cause. Scan for concrete signal words or punctuation and label Temporal, Contrast, or Cause-Effect.
